newsitem.title: UK: 30 years on, Aberfan survivors relive nightmare.
newsitem.headline: 30 years on, Aberfan survivors relive nightmare.

text.p: Survivors of the disaster that overwhelmed the primary school at Aberfan in south Wales 30 years ago on Monday still have nightmares about being buried alive in a sea of black mud.
Just 10 children were pulled to safely from the school that was obliterated by a collapsing coal tip on the morning of October 21, 1966.
"It felt like the end of the world," said Gaynor Madgwick, still battling to come to terms with the suffocating horror that robbed her of her childhood.
Then aged eight, she was saved from asphyxiation because a collapsed radiator shielded her and was finally rescued by her grandfather.

Her brother and sister were among the 116 children and 28 adults who were killed when the deadly black avalanche hurtled down the mountain at 50 miles an hour (80kph) and wiped out a generation of children in the tight-knit mining community.

"You don't want to remember because it brings back so many feelings of guilt and fear. Why was I lucky? Why me?" asked Jeff Edwards, the last child pulled out alive from the shattered wreckage of Pantglas school.
In the bitter recriminations that followed Britain's worst landslide disaster, the official tribunal pinned responsibility on the state-owned National Coal Board.
Aberfan's murderous Number Seven tip was found to have been built over a natural spring which soaked and destabilised the colliery waste as it if were on ball-bearings.
Survivors and relatives in the village that is in perpetual mourning were to mark the 30th anniversary of the disaster with a simple service in the hillside cemetery.
Articulating their grief has been an uphill battle for the survivors. The psychological scars still not have healed. Many fear sleeping in the dark. They feel guilty about being spared.
Survivor Gerald Kirwan said: "Here I am, a grown man, tough ex-miner and all that. Yet since that day I don't like the dark. Even being at home on my own at night makes me uneasy."
A grainy black and white photo of Susan Robertson being carried from the wreckage of the school by the village policeman was one of the few rays of hope amid so much darkness.
She, like the others, has started to express her anguish after years of bottling up the emotion. For a BBC documentary on the stricken village, she recalled the black day as if it was yesterday.
"I could just see daylight through the inkwell of my desk. Then they dug me out. All I could see was slurry on top of the school. I didn't know where I was," she said.
Gaynor Madgwick has helped fellow survivors to come to terms with the disaster by publishing the graphic account that she scribbled down in her school exercise book later she was 12.

"I didn't cry afterwards as I didn't know what was happening. It was all like a dream. Bodies lay crushed and buried," she wrote. "As I looked back, I saw my friends dead -- the last time for me to see them."
